header.intro:
Experienced Cybersecurity Consultant and Network Technician with a proven record in real-time technical support, network migration, and security protocol implementation. Skilled in vulnerability management, network troubleshooting, automation tooling, and advanced threat analysis for monitoring and incident response. Strong capability in data assessment and translating technical findings into actionable, business-aligned decisions.

My journey started in a small cybercafé installing and repairing computers. From there, I progressed to leading IT projects, then rebuilt my career from the ground up after relocating to Sweden with no local language and no certifications. Today, as a solution architect, I bring solid skills in cybersecurity and network infrastructure shaped by resilience, continuous learning, and hands-on experience.
header.tagline: Below are a set of security and network tools built around one theme: defending critical infrastructure through SIEM-driven detection, automation, and defense-in-depth.

flagship.name: CV Builder
flagship.description: A local first CV builder and job search assistant with 14 templates, a real time ATS score sidebar, PDF import and export, an application tracker, job matching, and an AI interview coach. Built to be the most complete resume tool for job seekers, not just a single purpose utility.

caseStudy.tagline: A local first CV builder and job search assistant, the flagship project
caseStudy.problem: Most resume builders are either generic templates with no feedback, or expensive subscriptions gatekeeping basic features like ATS scoring. Job seekers need one tool that covers the whole loop: building the CV, checking it against a real job description, tracking applications, and prepping for the interview.
caseStudy.approach: Built with Next.js and Supabase for auth and storage, with DeepSeek powering the AI features: a real time ATS score sidebar, tailoring suggestions against a pasted job description, a skill gap analyzer, salary insights, an AI interview coach, and a LinkedIn optimizer, on top of 14 templates and PDF import and export. I later moved it onto timfas.com at /cv-builder/ so it lives alongside my other tools instead of on its own domain.
caseStudy.decisions: I chose Supabase over a self managed database to keep auth, storage, and Postgres in one managed service for a solo built product, trading some vendor lock-in for a much smaller operational surface. I picked DeepSeek for the AI features over a larger frontier model provider mainly on cost per request at the volume a free tier tool needs to sustain, and wrote the interview coach and tailoring prompts to be portable to another provider if that tradeoff changes later.
caseStudy.lesson: Adding a basePath to a Next.js app to share a domain path is not just a config change: every internal client side fetch call to an API route has to be explicitly prefixed with that basePath, or it silently breaks in production while looking fine in development. That single class of bug was found across four separate features during an audit and became the reason a shared withAppBasePath() helper exists in the codebase now, so it cannot be forgotten again.

architectureNote.title: How these fit together
architectureNote.body: Each tool below maps to a layer of a defense in depth design: perimeter and email trust (inspect, cert-check), access and identity hygiene (passcheck), policy enforcement (acl-gen), and network segmentation (subnet-calculator). Built, deployed, and monitored the same way I would document and hand off a production architecture: with a clear problem statement, the tradeoffs behind each decision, and a lesson learned, all in the case study linked from every card.

platformCard.name: reference architecture
platformCard.description: How this portfolio itself is deployed: one Caddy reverse proxy with automatic TLS in front of static sites, small Node services, and a Next.js app, plus a cron based uptime checker feeding the status dots on every card.

footer: Built by Tim, one small tool at a time, shipped in phased increments with a public roadmap and change history.

projects.name: passcheck.
projects.description: A password strength and known breach checker that runs entirely in the browser. Checks breach status with the Have I Been Pwned API using k-anonymity, so the password never leaves the page in full.
projects.tagline: A password strength and known breach checker that never sends your password anywhere in full
projects.problem: People reuse weak passwords because strength meters are inconsistent and breach checking tools usually ask you to type your real password into a form you have to trust. That is a bad habit to encourage, even for a legitimate tool.
projects.approach: Password strength is scored entirely client side, so nothing about the password ever leaves the browser during analysis. Breach checking uses the Have I Been Pwned API with k-anonymity: only the first five characters of the password's SHA-1 hash are sent to the API, and the full match happens locally in the browser against the returned candidate list. The full password is never transmitted.
projects.impact: Compromised credentials are still the leading way attackers get in: Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found stolen or reused credentials involved in the majority of breaches it analyzed, and infostealer data shows most people reuse the same password across a large share of their accounts. The usual fix, a password strength meter or breach checker, asks people to type a real password into a form and trust a server with it, a bad habit to build even for a legitimate tool. passcheck. checks strength entirely in the browser and checks breach status using k-anonymity, so the password itself, and even its full hash, never leaves the device, free, for anyone.
projects.decisions: I chose the k-anonymity design, sending only a 5 character hash prefix and matching the rest locally, over the simpler option of hashing and sending the full SHA-1, because a full hash is still enough for the API operator to correlate requests to a specific password over time. The extra client side matching logic is a deliberate tradeoff: a little more code for a real, not just claimed, privacy guarantee.
projects.lesson: Privacy by architecture, not by policy, is the differentiator here. A privacy promise in a README is worth little if the code sends the raw password to a server anyway. Building the k-anonymity flow correctly was the whole point of the project, not an add-on feature.

projects.name: inspect.
projects.description: A DNS and security header inspector. Checks SPF, DKIM, and DMARC email authentication records and grades a site's security headers from A to F, with plain English explanations for each result.
projects.tagline: A DNS and security header inspector with plain English explanations
projects.problem: Email spoofing and missing security headers are two of the most common, most overlooked domain misconfigurations. Existing checkers either bury the result in jargon (raw SPF/DKIM/DMARC record dumps) or grade a site without explaining what the grade actually means for a non-specialist.
projects.approach: A small Express backend performs the DNS lookups for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and fetches security headers for the target site, then grades the headers A through F similar to Mozilla Observatory. Each result includes a plain English explanation of what it means and why it matters, added directly in response to the question "does 58 percent mean this site is not secure enough", since a percentage alone does not answer that.
projects.impact: Email spoofing and impersonation remain one of the costliest, most preventable categories of cybercrime: the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center attributes billions of dollars in annual U.S. losses to phishing and business email compromise, and independent DMARC adoption surveys consistently find that fewer than half of organizations enforce it strictly enough to actually block spoofed mail. Most of that gap is not malicious, it is that reading an SPF, DKIM, or DMARC record, or a security header report, requires specialist knowledge most domain owners never had a reason to learn. inspect. closes that gap for free: point it at any domain and get a plain English read on whether it can be spoofed and whether its headers protect visitors, no account, no jargon, no paywall.

source.label: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2025 Internet Crime Report

projects.decisions: I needed a small Express backend here, unlike the fully client side tools in this portfolio, because DNS lookups (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and header fetches against an arbitrary third party domain are blocked by browser CORS policy and would leak the visitor doing the lookup. That backend dependency is exactly why this was the one tool that went silently down, so I added it to the uptime checker that now polls every 5 minutes and drives the status dot on every project card.
projects.lesson: A backend service that looks fine can still die quietly. The systemd unit here has Restart=on-failure, but the process was stopped by a clean SIGTERM rather than a crash, so it did not auto-restart and sat dead for about 22 hours before a routine check caught it. A grading tool is only useful if it is actually up, this is a reminder to add real uptime monitoring, not just a restart policy.

projects.name: cert-check.
projects.description: An SSL/TLS certificate checker. See expiry countdown, chain of trust, protocol version, key strength, and hostname coverage for any domain, explained in plain English.
projects.tagline: An SSL/TLS certificate checker with plain English grading
projects.problem: Certificates expire quietly and cause outages at the worst possible time. Checking expiry, chain of trust, protocol version, and key strength normally means reaching for openssl on the command line, which most people outside networking or security do not use day to day.
projects.approach: A small backend connects to the target host over TLS, walks the certificate chain, and reports expiry countdown, chain of trust, negotiated protocol version, key strength, and hostname coverage (SAN matching), all translated into plain English rather than raw certificate fields.
projects.impact: Certificate expiry is one of the most common, most avoidable causes of outages on the internet: DigiCert's 2025 Trust Pulse Survey found close to half of organizations experienced certificate related downtime in the past year, with expired certificates the single largest cause, and some individual incidents running into the millions of dollars and hours of remediation. The fix is almost always trivial once someone notices in time, the hard part is that checking chain of trust, protocol version, and key strength normally means being comfortable with openssl on a command line. cert-check. reads the live handshake the same way a browser would and reports back in plain English, so anyone can catch a problem before it becomes an outage.
projects.decisions: I used a direct TLS socket connection to read the live certificate chain instead of relying on a third party certificate transparency log API, so the result always reflects exactly what a real client connecting right now would see, including misconfigurations like an incomplete chain that a log lookup alone would not surface. I chose accuracy over convenience here on purpose.
projects.lesson: The tool was scoped deliberately as a one shot checker, with no ongoing watchlist or email alerting. That kind of persistent monitoring feature is a real product on its own, and trying to build it here would have turned a focused, portfolio ready tool into an unfinished one.

projects.name: subnet.
projects.description: A clean, visual IPv4 subnet and CIDR calculator. Shows the network and host bit split, a full binary breakdown, and includes a VLSM subnet splitter and shareable links.
projects.tagline: A clean, visual IPv4 subnet and CIDR calculator
projects.problem: Most subnet calculators online just spit out a set of numbers. They are built for people who already understand subnetting, not for the students and junior admins who are trying to learn it. There is rarely an explanation of why the network and host bit split works the way it does.
projects.approach: Built as a single page app that runs entirely in the browser. Any IP and prefix combination is broken down visually: a network/host bit bar, a full binary breakdown of each octet, and the standard computed values (network address, broadcast, usable host range, wildcard mask). A VLSM splitter was added so a block can be divided into smaller subnets of different sizes in one view, and a permalink feature encodes the current calculation into the URL so a result can be shared or bookmarked directly.
projects.impact: There is a well documented cybersecurity and IT workforce shortage: the 2025 ISC2 Cybersecurity Workforce Study puts the global gap at roughly 4.8 million unfilled roles, with about 750,000 of those in the U.S. alone, and most organizations report that skills gaps directly contribute to security incidents. That gap starts earlier than most people think, subnetting is one of the first concepts that trips up students and junior admins, and most tools built for it assume you already understand it. subnet. was built for the other end of that curve: free, visual, and built to actually explain the network and host math, not just spit out an answer.
projects.decisions: I chose client side only, no backend, over a server side calculator because subnetting math does not need to touch a network at all. Doing it in the browser removes a whole class of availability and latency concerns for a tool that should feel instant. I encoded permalinks directly into the URL query string instead of storing them server side, trading a slightly longer URL for zero database, zero expiry, and zero privacy exposure of what someone calculated.
projects.lesson: IPv6 support was scoped out deliberately. It was tempting to add it early, but VLSM and shareable permalinks were more useful to more people and shipped faster. Keeping the feature set disciplined and finishing fewer things completely, rather than half-finishing more things, made this a stronger portfolio piece.

projects.name: acl-gen.
projects.description: A firewall rule and ACL syntax translator. Build a rule once and see Cisco IOS, pfSense, iptables, AWS, and Azure syntax side by side, plus shadowed rule detection and a packet tester.
projects.tagline: A firewall rule and ACL syntax translator across five vendor formats
projects.problem: The same firewall rule has to be re-written by hand in Cisco IOS, pfSense, iptables, and increasingly cloud formats like AWS security groups and Azure NSGs. Translating between them manually is slow and a common source of mistakes during migrations or audits.
projects.approach: A rule is defined once in a simple form, parsed into a single internal model, and rendered out to all five syntaxes side by side. Shadowed and conflicting rule detection flags rules that can never be reached, and a packet tester lets you simulate a packet against the rule set to see which rule matches and why, all before anything is deployed to real hardware.
projects.impact: Misconfiguration, not just novel attacks, causes a large share of real incidents: Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report attributes more than a quarter of breaches to errors and misconfigurations, concentrated heavily in cloud and network environments where the same rule has to be re-expressed correctly across multiple syntaxes. Firewall and ACL rules are a classic case, the same intent gets hand translated into Cisco IOS, pfSense, iptables, and cloud security groups, and small mistakes during that translation are a routine, avoidable source of exposure. acl-gen. defines a rule once and renders it correctly across five formats, with shadow and conflict detection built in, so the translation step stops being where mistakes get introduced.
projects.decisions: I designed a single internal rule model first, before writing any vendor renderer, so adding a sixth vendor format later only means writing one new renderer against an existing model instead of reworking the whole tool. Shadow and conflict detection runs against that same internal model rather than against each rendered syntax separately, so I write and test that logic once instead of five times.
projects.lesson: Four features (shadow detection, the packet tester, cloud syntax support, and shareable permalinks/export) were planned and shipped together in one focused pass rather than trickled out. Treating that as one milestone, not four separate small updates, made the tool feel complete rather than perpetually half built.
